strengths: The data construction pipeline is unusually rigorous for PR mining work: explicit noise taxonomy (Table 2), round-trip verification of Search/Replace blocks against a reconstructed post-PR state (Algorithm 1), and a multi-layered decontamination protocol (repo blocklist + SHA-256 exact file matching + 15-gram/Jaccard overlap) that goes beyond typical repo-name exclusion.

The resulting Clean-PR corpus (2M verified instances, 12 languages, 17.7B tokens) is substantially larger and more rigorously validated than prior natural code-change corpora (CommitPackFT, CodeReview) while retaining multi-file, real-task structure that those lack, per the comparison in Table 1.

Empirical results are strong and consistent: large absolute gains over the Instruct baseline (13.6% Lite, 12.3% Verified) and a clean, apples-to-apples ablation against a carefully re-implemented StarCoder2-style baseline (same raw data, different filtering/format) isolates the contribution of the Search/Replace + issue-linking design (Table 6, Table 8).

Multiple complementary ablations (edit format vs diff, issue augmentation vs PR-desc-only, Python-only vs multilingual, error-driven augmentation vs standard SFT, catastrophic-forgetting dynamics in Figure 2, Pass@k scaling in Figure 3) build a coherent and mostly convincing causal story for where the gains come from.

Strong reproducibility effort: extensive appendices detailing filtering heuristics, regex rules, language-extension tables, prompts for all three Agentless stages, training hyperparameters, and a proposed dataset release schema (Table 16).
weaknesses: All experiments use a single base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B); the paper explicitly defers cross-model generalization to future work (Appendix D), so it is unclear whether the recipe transfers to other architectures/scales or is entangled with Qwen-Coder-specific pretraining.

SWE-bench Lite (300) and Verified (500) are small evaluation sets, and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported for the headline Pass@1 numbers; given known run-to-run variance on SWE-bench-style benchmarks, some reported deltas (e.g., 1-3 point differences in ablations like Table 8/9) may not be statistically robust.

The error-driven augmentation pipeline generates hard negatives using the same base Instruct model family that is later fine-tuned and evaluated with an Agentless scaffold; this creates a degree of circularity (the negative distribution is shaped by the same model's failure modes) whose effect on generalization to genuinely novel distractor patterns is not analyzed.

The Agentless-aligned SFT stage relies on a comparatively small "Origin" set (~53K instances from SWE-rebench/SWE-Gym trajectories, Table 5), so the paper does not cleanly disentangle how much of the final performance comes from the 17.7B-token mid-training versus this smaller, benchmark-adjacent SFT set beyond the single Base+SFT vs Base+Mid-train+SFT contrast in Table 6.

Comparisons to external open-source baselines (Table 7) are limited to three systems with differing scaffolds (agentic OpenHands, SWESynInfer) and are copied from original papers rather than re-run under matched conditions, making the "outperforms 72B models" claim somewhat apples-to-oranges despite being an interesting result.

The work is primarily a data-curation and training-recipe contribution rather than a new algorithmic idea; while valuable and useful, the methodological novelty (Search/Replace conversion, stepwise SFT, hard-negative mining) largely combines and refines existing techniques (Xia et al. Agentless, StarCoder2 filtering methodology) rather than introducing fundamentally new methods.

Training cost is very high (259 GPU-hours × 32 H200 for mid-training alone), which limits practical reproducibility by other groups even though hyperparameters are disclosed; the actual public release of the full 3M-PR corpus is stated as a future action ("we will release") rather than confirmed at submission time.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and well-motivated question: how much repository-level editing capability can be internalized into model weights via training data, disentangling this from inference-time scaffolding complexity.

The data construction pipeline is rigorous and well-documented: bot filtering, core-language rules, issue linking, and a genuinely verifiable round-trip Search/Replace reconstruction (Algorithm 1) that guarantees bit-wise exact reconstruction, which is a meaningful improvement over noisy diff-based corpora.
Scale and diversity of the released corpus (2M verified PRs, 12 languages, 45K+ repos) substantially exceeds prior natural code-change corpora in structured, multi-file, verified form (Table 1).

Strong and consistent empirical gains over a carefully constructed, well-matched StarCoder2-style baseline (same token budget, same base model) isolate the contribution of data quality/format rather than just scale, and ablations (Table 8, Table 9) further decompose the sources of improvement (S/R format, issue linking, error-driven augmentation).

Non-trivial decontamination effort, including repo-level exclusion, SHA-256/n-gram matching, and an embedding-based semantic leakage analysis (Appendix A.7) showing no positive correlation between train-test similarity and resolve rate, which is more rigorous than typical practice.

Broad generalization studies (7B scale, multilingual Multi-SWE-bench, and OpenHands agentic transfer) show the learned capability is not narrowly overfit to the specific Agentless scaffold or model size used for the main results.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility documentation in the appendix (prompts, hyperparameters, filtering rules, dataset schema).
weaknesses: All experiments use a single base model family (Qwen2.5-Coder, 32B and 7B); it is unclear whether the Clean-PR recipe transfers to other architectures/tokenizers, and the paper explicitly defers this to future work.

No variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are reported for Pass@1 numbers on SWE-bench Lite/Verified, which are known to be sensitive to patch-application and grading nuances; single-run point estimates make it hard to assess the reliability of gains, especially smaller deltas in ablations.

External comparisons (Table 7) against SWE-Gym, Lingma-SWE, and SWE-Fixer are not fully controlled — these systems differ in training data, scaffolding, and possibly evaluation protocol/settings, so claims of 'surpassing 72B baselines' should be interpreted cautiously rather than as a controlled comparison.

The dataset is only 'planned' for release at submission time; given the paper's central claim rests on data quality/scale, reviewers cannot verify pipeline outputs or dataset statistics independently before release.

Filtering heuristics (bot regex patterns, keyword blocklists for titles/descriptions, core-file extension rules) are entirely heuristic; no human-annotated precision/recall validation of the noise-filtering pipeline is reported, so the true quality of the 'Clean' 18.59% subset is asserted rather than directly measured.

The Search/Replace edit format itself is adopted from prior work (Agentless/Xia et al.), so the core methodological novelty lies primarily in the data pipeline and training recipe rather than in a new modeling or algorithmic contribution.

Some explanatory claims (e.g., why multilingual training improves single-language SWE-bench performance) are speculative and not substantiated by deeper mechanistic analysis beyond aggregate score differences.

strengths: The data construction pipeline (bot/noise filtering, core-language rules, issue linking, and especially the round-trip verified Search/Replace conversion in Algorithm 1) is carefully engineered and clearly documented in the appendix, giving good transparency into how the 2-3M instance corpus was produced.

The empirical study is broad: internal ablations (mid-training vs. none, Clean-PR vs. StarCoder2-style format, Python-only vs. multilingual), error-driven augmentation ablation, scale generalization to 7B, multilingual evaluation on Multi-SWE-bench, and agentic transfer to OpenHands all point in a consistent direction and support the paper's core narrative.

The decontamination effort (repository exclusion, SHA-256 exact-match filtering, n-gram/Jaccard filtering, plus a semantic leakage analysis via embedding similarity quintiles) is more rigorous than typically seen in this literature and directly addresses an obvious reviewer concern.

The catastrophic-forgetting analysis (Figure 2, HumanEval/LiveCodeBench trajectories) is a nice addition showing the verified S/R format avoids degrading general coding ability relative to the noisy-diff baseline.
If released as promised, the corpus itself (Table 1) would be a useful community resource given its scale and the paucity of large verified multi-file PR-to-edit datasets.
weaknesses: The central thesis - that repo-level editing capability can be internalised primarily via PR-derived mid-training - is confounded by the fact that the Agentless-aligned SFT stage is built from existing curated benchmark trajectories (SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym), not from Clean-PR itself. This makes it hard to cleanly attribute the reported gains to the PR corpus versus the (also carefully engineered) SFT stage; the paper does not present a mid-training-only evaluation without any SFT to isolate this.

The Best-of-N results (Figure 3) show a large gap between Pass@1 (30.6%) and Pass@10 (41.5%) on Verified, undercutting the paper's framing that scaffolding/search is unnecessary once capability is 'internalised'; a substantial portion of the model's latent capability still requires external ranking/verification to surface, which is in tension with the stated motivation.

The comparison against SOTA open-source methods (Table 7) is thin and somewhat dated (SWE-Gym, Lingma-SWE, SWE-Fixer); no comparison is made against more recent, stronger 32B-class or RL-tuned SWE agents that were plausibly available at the time of writing, weakening the 'competitive with 72B models' claim.

Main results rely on single-run point estimates on relatively small benchmarks (300/500 instances) with no variance/error bars or multiple seeds reported, despite Pass@1 differences between settings sometimes being only a few points.

The noise-filtering heuristics (bot regexes, keyword blocklists, core-extension rules) are validated only by reporting how much data they remove (Table 2), not by any precision/recall check against human-labeled samples, so it is unclear how much valid signal is discarded or how much residual noise remains.

The error-driven augmentation negatives are generated using Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, the same model family used throughout the pipeline and as base model for the final system, raising a possible self-referential bias in what 'realistic' distractors look like that is not discussed or ablated against negatives from a different model family.
Dataset release is only promised ('we plan to release'), so reproducibility of the core contribution (the corpus) cannot currently be verified by reviewers or the community.

All experiments use a single base model family (Qwen2.5-Coder); no evidence is given that the Clean-PR recipe transfers to other LLM backbones, limiting confidence in the generality of the claimed data-centric findings.

strengths: Constructs the largest publicly-releasable PR-derived corpus (2M verified instances, 12 languages) via a rigorous, well-documented pipeline (bot/noise filtering, issue linking, Search/Replace reconstruction with round-trip byte-wise verification), addressing a genuine gap between noisy commit-level corpora and expensive SWE-bench-style datasets.

Extensive and carefully controlled ablations isolate the individual contributions of the pipeline: edit format (S/R vs. diff), issue-augmented context, error-driven augmentation, and multi-language vs. Python-only training, each showing consistent, interpretable gains.

Strong empirical results across multiple axes of generalization: 32B main results, 7B scale transfer, multilingual evaluation (Multi-SWE-bench Flash), and transfer into a different inference paradigm (OpenHands agentic loop), suggesting the learned capability is not merely overfit to the Agentless scaffold.

Thoughtful decontamination protocol (repo-level exclusion, SHA-256 exact matching, n-gram/Jaccard filtering, plus a semantic similarity/leakage correlation analysis) that goes beyond typical practice and helps substantiate that gains reflect generalization rather than leakage.

High reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with the verification algorithm, exact prompts for all three Agentless stages, hyperparameters, dataset schema, and a stated intent to release the dataset.

Efficiency story is compelling: the 32B model with simplified Agentless scaffolding outperforms larger 72B agentic baselines and a same-size OpenHands-trained baseline (SWE-Gym), supporting the central claim that data quality can substitute for scaffold complexity.
weaknesses: The primary baseline ('StarCoder2-style') is self-implemented by the authors rather than an existing published system, so the comparison, while described as faithful, could still embed implementation choices that indirectly favor Clean-PR; an independent or more standardized baseline would strengthen the claim.

Evaluation is confined to a single base model family (Qwen2.5-Coder); generalization to other pretrained backbones or tokenizers is explicitly left to future work, limiting confidence that the recipe is architecture-agnostic.

SWE-bench Lite/Verified are relatively small (300/500 instances) and results appear to be single runs without variance/seed reporting, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of reported gains (e.g., the ~2-3 point differences in some ablations).

The large Pass@1 vs. Pass@10 gap (Figure 3) indicates the likelihood-based decoding/ranking is a bottleneck the paper identifies but does not address, leaving the practical upper bound of the approach unexplored.

Comparisons to external 72B baselines (Table 7) rely on numbers copied from original papers under potentially different evaluation protocols/scaffolds, so the 'half the parameters, better performance' claim should be interpreted cautiously.

Issue-linking relies on simple regex heuristics over PR/issue text with no reported precision/recall for correct issue-PR association, leaving some uncertainty about how much noise remains in the 'issue-augmented intent' signal.
The dataset release is only 'planned,' so full reproducibility (beyond the algorithmic description) cannot yet be independently verified by reviewers or the community.
